blocks.title: Exact core
blocks.what: The engine that reads a GGUF file and generates text, written in C with no external libraries. «Exact» means the numbers it produces are identical to those of transformers, the Python reference: if we get it wrong, we know right away instead of noticing from strange answers.

blocks.title: SIMD kernels + tier
blocks.what: The heavy math (matrix multiplications) written in the CPU's vector instructions, with one version per family and the choice made at runtime. Every version gives the same bits as the scalar version, and a test verifies it.

numbers.v: OLMoE's routers are bf16 values saved as F32 (every low half zero): kept in bf16 at load, widened with a shift into the same lanes as the F32 product, same bits by construction. The router from 179-186 to 120-130 microseconds a token (1.40-1.48x), about 0.4% of the token

question 66, the Q4_K decode read as a genome: the scalar decoding of the scales was 24% of a row. Scales in vector one block ahead and two weight rows per call, same bits: in L1 1.25x and 1.38x; from RAM at 4 threads llama.cpp goes from 1.37x to 1.04x; the real model at 4 threads generates 50.4 tok/s against llama.cpp's 50.2 (was 40.3): even, and exact

generation, one token at a time, against llama.cpp's kernels from RAM: on Q8_0 even at 4 threads (0.97-1.06x, both at the memory ceiling), theirs 1.4-1.7x at one thread; on Q4_K theirs 1.34-1.40x at 4 threads and even from 8, because our exact math does 9.3 GB/s per core. Three exact kernels tried and closed with a no (four rows together 0.5-0.9x from RAM)
more weight rows per token load (4 x 6 and 3 x 8): pure math goes as today, but in the real matmul loses 6-16%; closed with a no, the matmul is not held back by the token load as we thought
decoding the weights once per row and then F32 across all tokens (ik_llama.cpp's idea, kept exact): Q8_0 1.00-1.04x, Q4_K 1.1x, closed
llama.cpp's kernels alone, on our own shapes, one core: on Q8_0 experts ours are 1.42x faster (102 against 72 GFLOP/s); on dense projections theirs 1.6x (8-bit integers), on reordered Q4_K 1.26-2.3x

two weight rows against 8 tokens at a time, and the final lane sum in SIMD: the matmul on one core from 87 to 102 GFLOP/s; native prefill 1.15-1.19x at 512 and 2048 tokens, 1.13-1.14x at 4000, generation unchanged, numbers identical to the bit
two weight rows per activation load: prefill 1.20-1.26x (Q8_0), 1.11x (Q4_K_M), generation unchanged, numbers identical to the bit
dot_row q8_0: from 1 957 to 19 837 M elements/s (AVX-512)
F16 rows with the tier's kernel: 49x

questions.text: reach llama.cpp at 4 threads on Q4_K decode while staying exact? reached: 50.4 against 50.2 tok/s

blocks.title: Thread pool and per-phase width
blocks.what: The laptop's cores used with no waste: the prompt on all of them, generation on the width the session measures for itself. The decode does not use every core because the limit is memory, not compute.

numbers.v: A/B inside a single process (generate --ab): alternating passes between two paths in the same file, 0.28% precision in two minutes; the arms with no period, because A B B A always put the KV's new pages on arm A (every 8 positions)

the chosen token's argmax, first on a single thread (116-118 microseconds a token, found by the pensatore), now split across the pool's threads with the same indices: 5.6-6.9 microseconds, a token about 0.7% faster, a 3-row verify pass 1.0175x. Outside the in-process A/B it did not run: a session field never cleared kept the serial scan (LESSONS #252); fixed on the evening of the 27th, every run now 5.5 microseconds

every verify pass size (2-4 rows) measures on its own how many threads to use, like the decode, skipping the narrowest width: on 16 cores it picks 8 threads in 16 runs out of 16; Q8_0 3.4-3.9% faster than the full pool and up to 5.7% of the decode's width. Also trying the narrowest cost Q4_K 2%: every 4-thread trial cost +60%

the prompt from 8 to 16 threads scales 1.49-1.50x natively on Q4_K, like llama.cpp in the race (1.44-1.49x): the 1.11-1.16x gap was the container with Q8_0. At 16 threads the tails are 17-20% of the time (slower cores, fixed regions): stealing work in tile blocks was proposed, not built

the decode's experts now split across threads in a balanced way too (the condition never caught them, 8 rows in 64 groups). On a free machine: generation 1.04-1.08x at 8 threads, the token reads at 51-52 GB/s out of 53-55 of RAM, RAM idle drops from 5-11% to 1-4% of the token; same bits
prompt on the whole pool, decode on the measured width: 1.05-1.09x
SMT makes it worse: 32 threads against 16 -> decode 2.2 against 22.9 tok/s
real SMT (native): two threads per core give the decode +1.6-5.7% at 4 cores, nothing at 8 (the width the engine picks, 60 tok/s), a collapse at 16 (8.4 against 58.3 tok/s)

the pool's tail: at 8 threads in the container it waited for the slowest thread for a fifth of every multiplication; with blocks stolen from the others, same bits: -8% of time in decode calls, native even

idle workers that prefetch into cache the start of the call after: in the bench 1.02-1.14x per call after a serial step of 1.5-6 us; in the engine even (12 runs: 0.996 ± 0.004): the serial step after every hint costs as much as the call gains. Turned off, ready to turn back on

what lies past the end of a thread's region: a guard page makes the dense call 0.8% faster, a thread's regions one after the other 1.0-1.75%; the experts nothing (0.2-0.4% of a token, in the dense layout)

pretouch: the calling thread asks for its own next lines before each hint. Even (8 runs: 1.003 ± 0.002) and the first norm still slowed by 54 us a token: a serial step under the workers' flood does not pay for its own lines. Out
piece 4: q, k, v in one call of the pool, and gate, up in one, their work spread as one range over the threads: generation 0.54% faster (12 runs: 1.0054 ± 0.0007), the same bits

questions.text: the width estimator rewritten: at 512 on native Q4_K it picks 8 cores in 6 runs out of 6, matching 8 forced; long context is missing
SMT in the decode: two threads per core beat llama.cpp on the same 4 cores? no: +1.6-5.7% at 4 cores, nothing at 8, where the engine works
why do 32 threads on 16 cores make the decode collapse (8.4 against 58.3 tok/s)?
gate and up interleaved at load? no: on a free machine 1.006-1.023x, the three calls already read at 97-98% of RAM

the serial steps as messages between cores: if they stop touching the workers' rows (add and mix inside the calls, normed and the prepared row in unread buffers), do the hints to idle workers pay off? (2026-10-02: pretouch, the steps' own lines asked ahead, even: the cost is not their misses)

blocks.title: KV with positions in a row
blocks.what: The context memory laid out so the CPU reads it in sequence instead of jumping around. Long context was the worst case: now it reads at RAM speed.

numbers.v: the KV pages touched by the pool right before the pass writes them (every stream starts at a page's start): kv_write from 80 to 50 microseconds a token, generation +0.17%, first prompt +0.4%, same bits. Touching them ahead of time instead cost the attention 2.4%: pages present past the streams' end slow reads by 1-2.4%
2 MB pages for weights and KV in the container (where the race runs): on a free machine no gain; closed

decode at long context against llama.cpp, read as a line: even with no context, 5.3 against 3.2 microseconds per position in memory. It's the bytes of their 16-bit KV: exact at 32 bit would need 81 GB/s, RAM gives 53-57. Our attention already reads at the speed of a pure read; on the GPU, same bits, we pass them (1.31x at 2048)
KV compressed to 28 bit, on a still machine: 0.97-1.05x the F32 attention; the decoding eats up the saved bytes (44-45 GB/s against 49-51): no on the CPU
in the KV only layer 0's values depend on the token alone (they repeat in 62-82% of positions); layers 1-15 and every key: 0 repeats
skipping positions exactly: closed before writing a kernel, OLMoE's attention is flat and even an oracle skips at most 0.2% of the bytes
decode one position at a time: exact, kept; on a still machine on the token it's indistinguishable (0.96-1.05x, the -9% zone at 2048); the bench gave 1.10-1.13x under load
context 2048: the gap with llama.cpp (1.16-1.26x) was the 32-bit KV against their 16-bit one (518 against 259 MiB per token); 16-bit KV is a no (Marcello, 2026-09-24: exact only)
decode at context 4000: 1.15-1.18x; the zone goes from 32-35 to 47-48 GB/s

questions.text: does the same overrun past a stream's end also cost the weights? yes, ~0.8% of a dense call (a guard page after each thread's region), nothing to the experts; a thread's regions one after the other 1.0-1.75%: the lever goes with piece 4 (q, k, v in one call)
pass llama.cpp in the long-context decode with the exact KV? on the CPU no (needs 81 GB/s), on the GPU yes

blocks.title: Prompt in blocks + grouped attention
blocks.what: The prompt is not processed one token at a time but in blocks of 512, so the matrices are large and the cores work full. It is also the piece the per-layer order (M1) will need to reorganize.

numbers.v: phase-major (the pensatore's idea): the contract's lane p is a chain in time, 16 weight rows run as SIMD lanes with the same bits; the tile does 164.7 GFLOP/s per core (98.6% of the float peak); Q4_K prompt at 4 threads 140 -> 218-223 tok/s (llama.cpp 222), at 16 threads 369 -> 575; Q8_0 at 16 threads 390-419 -> 550-569; logits identical to the byte

softmax's and SwiGLU's exponential in vector (AVX-512 and AVX2, no FMA): 0 differences on all 2^32 floats at every level; on a free machine the prompt's attention 1.34-1.37x and the prefill 1.05x at 2048 and at 4000 tokens

the prompt's attention in tiles (4 queries by 4 positions, lane sums in vector): its zone 1.31-1.33x in the engine, the prefill 1.03x at 2048 tokens and 1.06x at 4000; the real model's logits identical to the byte
prefill from 30.1 to 196.9 tok/s (blocks + 4-token kernel)
grouped attention on long prompts: 1.09-1.13x

exact sums at the float's speed (Marcello's challenge, with the pensatore in shifts): W16, Winograd's trick (1968) in 16-bit words with the sub-block's scale inside the weight, identical bit for bit to an exact integer definition, does 167.2 GFLOP/s against the float tile's 164.7 (and 1.21x at equal width): exact and at least as fast as float, in the tile. On the RTX 4070's int8 tensor cores: 59.1 T-MAC/s exact against 3.29 of float, E32 there 4.5x

Q4_K in exact integers in the engine (W16): prompt 1.001x and decode 1.006x against float, measured alternated; logits identical at 4 and 16 threads and between prompt and decode; the oracles on the real cut model 1-26% closer to the reference. The predicted +10% on the experts did not arrive: in the engine the W16 tiles yield ~0.83 of the microbench

questions.text: E32 as the definition? Marcello: yes, in stages. Stage 1 measured (the W16 pieces on the engine's layouts), stage 2 done: Q4_K in exact integers in the engine, at float speed in prompt and generation; stage 3 is the GPU with tensor cores (question 74)
the softmax's exponential in vector: built, same bits as tr_expf; prefill +5%

blocks.title: Correctly-rounded tr_expf
blocks.what: The C library's exponential cost 30% of the long prompt. Rewritten: faster and correctly rounded across all 4 billion floats, checked one by one.

numbers.v: against the references, on all 2^32 floats: llama.cpp/ggml's exp misrounds 3.36% of the time (up to 2 ulp), glibc's 0.004%, ours never

the exact exp with floats only, in AVX-512 and AVX2: 0 different across all 4 billion floats, 4.8x and 4.4x faster than tr_expf per value; the prompt would only gain 2-3% from it: it stays the reference for the GPU
prefill 1.03-1.31x depending on length; Windows and Linux now give the same bytes

questions.text: SIMD version: no, the scalar one has already taken almost everything
the exact exp with floats only in SIMD: 4.8x per value; wired into the engine on 09/26 (question 70: softmax and SwiGLU)

blocks.title: The model read as a genome
blocks.what: Looking at every byte of the model, the context memory and the experts' choices, to find exact structure nobody reads: repeats, zeros, predictable parts. Where it exists, it is exploited without changing a single bit; where it does not, we know it and do not go back.

numbers.v: a token's timeline (tools/token_timeline.py): RAM stays idle 12-15% of the token, almost all of it waiting for the slowest thread at the end of calls, not between calls (0.6%)
the low 16 bits of the context memory do not decide the token: 1 token changed out of 1792
quantized weights are nearly incompressible: Q8_0 codes carry 7.6-7.7 bit out of 8, Q4_K 3.83-3.87 out of 4 (lossless compression ~7% and ~4%): closed
repeated blocks 0.008%: the output head's 220 identical rows are the tokens the model never learned
tools ready for the next model: tools/weights_genome.py, route_union_report.py, kv_repeats_report.py, draft_agreement.sh

questions.text: how much do the weights compress losslessly? ~7% Q8_0, ~4% Q4_K: not worth a format
is there exact structure in the model? only in the dead vocabulary and in layer 0's values

the most likely token from the output head's high half, exact only on the rows that can still win. Measured (10-05): the high half of each weight already rules out 96-99.8% of the 50304 rows; the head read at 0.53 of its bytes, a token 1.039x on the machines limited by their RAM (Q8_0), 1.017x (Q4_K). To build and race

blocks.title: Review and gate
blocks.what: Review of the GGUF reader, the expert store, the pool, the platform and the gate (09/22), then of the model, the kernels, the tokenizer and the command line (09/23). On the 23rd: the command line sized -n and -p buffers (an overflow near 2^62) and truncated --tokens to 32 bit; three OLMoE options had never been checked against transformers (now there is an oracle for it); memory pressure in Docker's VM counted as killed mutants. Then read the survivors of tokenizer.c (75 -> 43) and of main.c (334 -> 43), all named: the command line has a single option parser, with numbers kept within their range (-n abc exits with 2), and test_cli tries every command. The mutation tool no longer hides survivors behind load timeouts and memory refusals, kills an expired check along with everything it launched (seven orphan processes had slowed and skewed a campaign), and is fast enough to run after every change (CHANGED=HEAD mutates only the changed lines). Still left out of mutate_files.sh: gguf.c, experts.c, threads.c and platform.c, and the measurement scripts still to move to the new machine rule (the machine-still file).

blocks.title: Slot store + LRU
blocks.what: The experts' pantry. It keeps in RAM as many experts as fit the budget; when one that is missing is needed, it reads it from disk and drops the one unused the longest. It works because two nearby tokens ask for almost the same experts.

numbers.v: 1024 (layer, expert) units of 6.375 MiB: 6528 MiB in all
3.6-4.0 experts out of 8 shared with the previous token

blocks.title: Budget in the engine
blocks.what: The engine takes experts from the store instead of from RAM, and `--expert-budget` says how much RAM to give it. With any budget the numbers produced are identical to the byte: the budget changes speed, never the result.

numbers.v: logits identical to the byte from full budget to minimum budget

blocks.title: Direct read from disk
blocks.what: Reads skipping the operating system's cache. Without it, the model would sit in RAM twice and every measurement would tell the speed of RAM instead of disk.

numbers.v: the system cache would inflate the prompt by 2.42x and generation by 1.35x
the disk at its limit: 1.9 GB/s at 2 MiB requests, 3.5 at 64 MiB (the request's size is the lever, not the order or the readers); BitLocker takes 3.8 more processors at 3.5 GB/s

blocks.title: Automatic plan
blocks.what: At startup it looks at how much RAM is free and picks the budget by itself, refusing to start if it would leave the machine without memory. No option to learn: that is the milestone's criterion.

blocks.title: M1's measurements
blocks.what: Four sessions on a still machine to find out what reading experts from disk really costs. They disproved the simulation M1 had been designed around, and found the prompt's waste.

the prompt: 306.9 tok/s with the model in RAM, 80-84 with any partial budget

blocks.title: Per-layer order in the prompt
blocks.what: The prompt is processed in blocks of 512 tokens. Before, every block went through every layer, so under budget it reread every expert from disk at every block. Now the loops are inverted -- for each layer, every block -- and each expert is read only once per prompt. Same exact numbers: only how many times it waits for the disk changes.

numbers.v: prompt 2048 at 50% budget: 6 273 MiB read instead of 22 880
prefill 12.41 s instead of 23.51: 1.89x, compute indistinguishable
at prompt 512 (a single pass) nothing changes, as expected

questions.text: does the prompt read the experts once per prompt? no, once per pass

blocks.title: The first prompt's cost
blocks.what: Under budget every startup rereads the model from disk. `trochilus serve` keeps the engine on (threads, model, expert store) between commands, and `run`, `chat`, `generate` run inside it on their own when it is up, with the same output to the byte. Measured: with the model fully in RAM the first prompt goes from 12.8 to 7.8 seconds, the load disappears. At half budget almost nothing (13.0 -> 12.0 s): every prompt rewrites the store from scratch, so there the lever is what to drop during the prompt. While the model loads a rainbow water bar shows (variant A). The disk at its limit: a layer's consecutive experts are read in one request a part (96 requests for the whole model instead of 3072), into slot pages faulted beforehand over the pool. Next: reading while you type (question 48).

numbers.v: with the server, model fully in RAM: first prompt 12.79 -> 7.81 s (removing the 4.98 s of loading)
with the server, half budget: 13.00 -> 12.04 s (0.926x), 139 fewer misses out of 1157
through the server: same stdout to the byte for every command, model loaded once
the bar: 63 mutations out of 63 caught by the tests

half budget, a first prompt: 321 tokens 4.39 -> 2.81 s (1.564x), 2048 tokens 1.090x; the 8 GB machine emulated 1.350x and 1.029x (its long prompt is compute)

blocks.title: Disk and compute together
blocks.what: Before, the engine read, then computed, then read again: disk and cores waited on each other in turn. Now, in the long prompt, a separate thread reads the next layer's experts from disk while the cores compute the current one. Same numbers to the byte: only when the data arrives changes. Since 10-03 a short prompt (one pass, up to 512 tokens) reads ahead too, in short requests, and what the next layer does not ask is dropped before it is read.

numbers.v: prompt 2048 at half budget: 11.45 -> 9.39 s (1.22x), the computed ceiling was 1.61x
at 512 tokens nothing: a single-block prompt does not read ahead (ceiling 1.40x)

one pass of 321 tokens on the 8 GB machine: 1.29x (Q4_K), 1.21x (Q8_0); 43-58 units dropped unread

blocks.title: The decode's attention on the GPU
blocks.what: The slowest piece of the long-context decode, the attention, runs on the GPU with the same bits as the CPU: every operation rounded like the definition, no fusions. The driver opens while the program is running: whoever has no GPU does not notice. A laptop puts the GPU to sleep between layers: a single thread group keeps it awake.

numbers.v: one layer at context 2048: 168 us against the CPU's 704; at 4000: 305 against 1415
logits identical to the byte through the engine: 2000 decode positions, tokens past 4000, a speculative round
decode in the engine, A/B on a still machine: 1.31-1.32x at 2048, 1.54-1.58x at 4000 (predicted 1.29 and 1.57); the token at 4000 from 44.8 to 29.8 ms

questions.text: keeping it awake costs 12-17 W while generating: always, or only from the context where it pays off?

blocks.title: Speculative decoding
blocks.what: Guessing several tokens at once by reusing pieces of the prompt, and checking them all together. The same tokens as before, only faster when the text repeats -- as it does in code.

blocks.title: The three machines and the theoretical limit
blocks.what: Every number of the rung measured on four machines, the weaker ones emulated on this PC: below average (4 threads, AVX2 only, 8 GB, an integrated GPU), average (8 threads, 16 GB, an integrated GPU only), average with a small dedicated GPU, this PC. The emulation gives fewer cores and less memory, never another GPU: an integrated GPU's numbers stay estimates until real PCs are available. Each machine's limit is its RAM's bandwidth divided by the bytes read a token; the engine is pushed toward it. On 8 GB the Q8_0 model (7 GB) needs its experts from disk. Measured on 10-03: the average machine and this PC are at their RAM's limit; the weak one was not. Its two brakes went the same night: the memory set aside for the run's own tokens instead of 4096, and ds4's rule for which expert leaves the RAM (replayed on the real routes before it was built): 3x its decode, with its disk emulated at a SATA-class 0.5 GB/s. The same day AVX2 got a Q4_K tile of its own (the weights decoded once for a group of tokens, in exact integers): the weak machine's Q4_K prompt 1.7x, its cores' 3.8x. Then its prompt waited for the disk 73% of its time: a second read in flight gives its one-queue disk nothing, but a prompt that fits one pass now reads each next layer while this one computes and drops what that layer does not ask: the prompt 1.21-1.29x, at 97-98% of the time its disk needs for its bytes. Then its first tokens after a prompt: the experts the prompt chose most now stay in RAM (ds4 counts a prompt's choices; ours had counted each expert once): its generation 8.00 -> 15.50 tok/s (Q4_K), 1.91 -> 2.38 (Q8_0). Left on it: chat's memory, a better eviction.

numbers.v: the same prompt and 64 tokens on the three machines, the same tokens on all of them: Q4_K generates 6.8 / 69.5 / 72.7 tok/s (weak / average / this PC), Q8_0 2.1 / 40.8 / 41.4; the average machine draws 103-108% of what its RAM gives, this PC 55-56 GB/s (its practical ceiling), the weak one 58-66% of its limit
on 8 GB the Q8_0 keeps 83 experts in RAM, fewer than the 128 a token uses: the least-recently-used rule then finds none of them (0 hits in 9010), 816 MiB a token from disk
this PC decodes at 98-99% of what its RAM gives in practice (56.3 GB/s measured, 68% of the nominal 83)

the eviction replayed on the real routes before it was built: with 83 experts in RAM the least-recently-used rule hits 0 of the 128 a token uses, keeping the first layers 10, ds4's rule 47, the unreachable best 65

on the 8 GB machine with its disk emulated (0.5 GB/s): the memory planned on the run's own tokens (Q8_0: 290 experts in RAM instead of 83) and ds4's rule take generation from 0.57 to 1.70 tok/s (Q8_0) and from 2.52 to 8.02 (Q4_K), the same tokens in every run

AVX2's own Q4_K tile (the W16 panel in two halves, tiles of 3: a tile of 4 runs out of registers): the 8 GB machine's Q4_K prompt 20.6 -> 35.1 tok/s with its disk, 36.4 -> 137.9 with every expert in RAM; two races, each against the binary before, the same tokens in all 68 runs; the decode unchanged

a one-pass prompt reads the next layer ahead in short requests and drops the unasked: the 8 GB machine's prompt Q4_K 35.3 -> 45.5 tok/s, Q8_0 20.3 -> 24.6, 2-3% more bytes, at 97-98% of its disk's time for them; the same tokens in all 24 runs, the decode unchanged

the prompt's routings told to the eviction (scaled to 64 tokens; ds4 adds them whole, ours of 10-03 added 1 a pass): on the 8 GB machine disk a decode token 42.9 -> 14.0 MiB (Q4_K), 233.8 -> 184.9 (Q8_0); generation 8.00 -> 15.50 tok/s (Q4_K), 1.91 -> 2.38 (Q8_0), the same tokens

a chat's memory for its whole context (4096 tokens, 1 GiB) no longer set aside at load: the experts hold it and hand it to the conversation a page at a time as it is written, which none of colibri, ds4 or llama.cpp does; on the 8 GB machine a chat keeps 278 Q8_0 experts instead of 131 and reads 194 MiB a token from disk instead of 376 (Q4_K 591 instead of 314, 16 instead of 87), and generates 2.29 tok/s instead of 1.22 (Q4_K 14.77 instead of 4.55), the same tokens

the same idea offered to colibri, built in its fork and raced on its own engine (OLMoE int8, a 5 GB container): 26 experts a layer instead of 16, 37% fewer expert reads, a request 1.19x faster, the logits byte-identical; less than ours because colibri reads through the system's file cache, which already used part of that room; opened as colibri's pull request #1873 on 2026-10-04, waiting for its review

the eviction told what is coming, replayed on the real routes: the unreachable best (Belady) needs 4-16 tokens of the future (Q8_0 on 8 GB: 33.75 expert misses a token today, 28.68 knowing the next token, 23.09 knowing 4, 18.35 knowing 16 = Belady); the next layer's router as a hint gives 0.3%, the text's own repeats see only 1-2 tokens, three rules from the past and quotas a layer lose or tie. Today's rule is the best that needs no future: closed

reading experts ahead on the 8 GB machine, modelled on the real routes before any code: the next layer's router reading its experts during this layer's compute gives 1.066x (Q4_K), because one layer's compute (2.2 ms) is a third of one expert's read (7.1 ms); computing a layer's experts already in RAM while its missing one is read gives 1.084x (Q4_K) and 1.038x (Q8_0) with no byte more; both 1.129x

built: a layer's missing experts read by a second thread while the experts already in RAM compute, the late ones computed as they land; the same bytes from disk, the same bits: on the 8 GB machine generation 14.98 -> 16.08 tok/s (Q4_K, 1.073x) and 2.33 -> 2.40 (Q8_0, 1.030x) in three races, the prompt unchanged; ds4 does it on its GPU from three misses only, which replayed here keeps almost nothing (1.004x)

the same binary run in each of its three ways, whole processes: computing each late expert as it lands is the best way on both models (Q4_K 1.079x, Q8_0 1.025x against the old way, two waves 1.073x and 1.015x); the threads handing work to each other cost 0.16% of a run

the router's read ahead (10-05): at a layer's router the next layer's router guesses its experts, 27 MiB of them read in pieces, a guess the next layer does not ask stopped mid-read, one it asks read whole from then on: the 8 GB machine's generation 1.031x (Q4_K), 1.000-1.005x (Q8_0), the same tokens; colibri's predictor replayed: its norm the same, its average 4.3 points worse; two layers ahead predicted at 74% and no gain

question 94, measured and modelled, not built: a draft that uses only the experts already in RAM guesses the next 8 tokens well on code (89-98% for the first) and badly on prose (50-88%); but checking its guesses costs more disk than it saves, because the expert store already reuses what neighbouring tokens share: every machine would lose (0.74-0.98x by the model). What survives: a draft that costs nothing, on the 8 GB machine's Q4_K (question 95)

questions.text: a decode layer's experts computed as their bytes arrive: built and raced (10-05): 1.073x (Q4_K) and 1.030x (Q8_0) on the 8 GB machine, against the model's 1.084 / 1.038

why the arrival order's arm slowed in one process: the handoffs measured cheap (11-13 us a take, 0.16% of a run) and whole processes of one binary agree with the races; the in-process A/B's alternation was its own (LESSONS #318)

the router's read ahead on top of the arrival order: built and raced (10-05): 1.031x (Q4_K) and 1.000-1.005x (Q8_0) on the 8 GB machine; whole-unit reads lose, pieces stopped when not named gain, a guess named is read a part a request (MEASUREMENTS §The router's read ahead)
the read ahead raced against the old binary (Smart App Control held 12147b2 all of 10-05) and on the average machine's Q8_0 (a 2 GB/s disk)

a draft from the bytes the machine already holds (Marcello, 10-05): phase 1 done, not built. The draft from the store's experts agrees 0.89-0.98 on code, 0.50-0.88 on prose (measured, chains of 8 from the exact state); every machine loses by the model on those chains (0.74-0.98x): the store already gives the saving a pass's shared experts promised, and a pass's rejected rows are read from disk twice (MEASUREMENTS §A draft from the bytes the machine holds)

the drafts that cost nothing (the lookup, the gate) on the 8 GB machine's Q4_K, where a token is half disk, half compute and a verify row may cost a fraction of a token: the model gives 1.02-1.40x with the resident draft's chains; first that machine's row price

blocks.title: The integrated GPU
blocks.what: Nearly every PC has a GPU inside its processor (Intel Iris Xe or UHD, AMD Radeon), sharing its RAM. It adds little to generation, which waits on the RAM or the disk, but the prompt is compute, and there it could give 3-5x on the 8 and 16 GB machines. Through Vulkan, loaded as a module like CUDA, the weights read where they already are (no copy: they share the RAM), the same bits as the CPU, and the CPU wherever a GPU cannot give them. After the 8 GB machine's two brakes, removed on 10-03 (3x its decode). Until real PCs are available, its numbers are estimates (question 88): this PC's Radeon 610M checks the bits, not the speed.

questions.text: what the integrated GPU gives on a real 8 or 16 GB laptop: until one is available, every number is an estimate

blocks.title: Generation's fixed cost
blocks.what: Under budget the first tokens after the prompt cost more: about one second, once, at 25% of the model in RAM. With the model fully in RAM it does not happen, so it is not the engine warming up: it is the expert store settling after the prompt. We know where it is, not yet exactly what it is.

numbers.v: resident: 34.64 tok/s at 200 tokens, 33.48 at 1000 -- no fixed cost
the extra misses of the first tokens explain ~115 ms out of 840

questions.text: where does the rest of the fixed cost go: a per-zone profile of the first 64 tokens

blocks.title: Server
blocks.what: A process that stays up and answers several requests. It fits together with the store surviving the session: it is the same problem seen from another angle.

blocks.title: Qwen3-MoE exact on a tiny model
blocks.what: The architecture's new pieces (GQA 32/4, 128 experts with 8 used, a norm per head) against transformers on random weights, the same way OLMoE's tiny oracle began.

blocks.title: Qwen's tokenizer and template
blocks.what: The tokenizer.json and the chat template, each against its reference.

blocks.title: Fewer bytes a weight: Q2_K, IQ2
blocks.what: Left: Q2_K and IQ2_XXS, the fewest bytes a weight, for the weaker machines (Q4_K and Q6_K done, Q4_K_M runs). Formats that hold the weights in fewer bytes (Q4_K, Q6_K, Q2_K, IQ2_XXS): less disk and less RAM, a lever that adds to all of M1. Done on 09/24: Q4_K and Q6_K in the engine, exact against their dequantized weights (identical to the bit to gguf-py, the real models cut to 2 layers against transformers in make check). Q4_K has our own AVX-512 kernel (a sub-block's 16 values computed once); Q6_K unpacks a block's 256 quants once and then runs like Q8_0. With Q6_K, Q4_K_M runs, the file people download. The real models in Q4_K and Q4_K_M are made from our own Q8_0, with no download. Measured again: in the prefill decoding the weights does not matter, loading the activations does, so no row dequantized once per block (dropped) and instead two weight rows per load (kept). On 09/25 the Q4_K decode at 4 threads reached llama.cpp (scales in vector, two rows per call). Next: the two rows also on AVX2. Two threads per core (SMT) in the decode: measured on 09/25, not worth it at the width the engine uses.

blocks.title: KV checkpoint on disk
blocks.what: Saving the context memory of a file already read, so reopening it does not cost a whole new prompt. It is the biggest lever for anyone always working on the same files.

questions.text: does reloading the KV cost less than the prefill? and does an 8-bit KV change the tokens?

blocks.title: The real model on the three machines
blocks.what: The ~17 GB download announced first; then the five phases on the three machines, coding prompts.

blocks.title: File reorder by co-activation
blocks.what: Rewriting the GGUF putting close together the experts that light up together (mbolt's idea, MIT). On our disk and with our large experts it is worth little: their own README says the gain fades above 4 MB per chunk, and ours are 6.4.

numbers.v: co-activation exists and grows with depth: at layers 8-15, 17-21% of pairs light up together more than double the baseline case; an expert's 3 most frequent companions make up 18-28% of its paired activations (baseline: 4.8%)
ceiling <= 1.15x here (from our own disk bench), against the 2.23x they claim on their own reads

blocks.title: Dense weights on the GPU
blocks.what: The matrices every token reads in full (attention and output head, about 395 MB a token) in VRAM, next to the KV. The Q8_0 matrix-vector product on the GPU gives the same bits as the CPU.

numbers.v: Q8_0 exact product at 97% of VRAM bandwidth; a token's dense weights 2.4 ms against ~7.7 on the CPU
model: 1.64x at 2048, 1.92x at 4000 together with the attention

after: exact integer Q4 on the GPU as a draft, checked exact by the engine. Q4_K picks Q8_0's token in 88.7 / 94.7 / 90.6% of cases (prose, code, italian): below the hoped-for 95%, but a 9-row verify pass reads only 3.52x a token's experts, so ~2x fewer bytes a token

blocks.title: Experts in VRAM
blocks.what: The GPU as a loadable module, not a dependency: whoever does not have one does not notice. The hottest experts in VRAM, the rest in RAM and on disk, with a single plan deciding what goes where.

numbers.v: model: with the experts fitting in VRAM ~4x at 2048 (9.3 ms a token against 36.8)

questions.text: an exact exp with float32 only for the GPU (the prefill wants billions of them, and doubles there run at 1/64)

blocks.title: The experts at the drive's limit, the VRAM as their cache
blocks.what: R3's candidate is Qwen3.8-Flash-Next FP8: 185 GB, 48 layers x 512 experts of 4.9 MB, 10 a token a layer. On a laptop with an 8 GB GPU and 31 GB of RAM almost every expert comes from the disk, so the speed is how fast the store reads them and how many the VRAM keeps as a cache below the RAM's. Not before R2 closes (one rung at a time).

numbers.v: colibri on this laptop: decode 0.75-1.01 tok/s, disk-bound; it reads the experts buffered at 0.6 GB/s, queue depth ~1.5, against 2.1-3.0 GB/s O_DIRECT on the same drive
VRAM gives more as expert cache than as trunk compute: the trunk in VRAM decodes 14% below the CPU, the VRAM all for experts 13% above; it holds ~5% of the experts (1248 of 24576), the RAM ~9%

questions.text: how close to the drive's limit can our store read 4.9 MB experts, and how many misses a token does the VRAM save as a cache tier under the RAM's

blocks.title: DeepSeek V4 Flash
blocks.what: A second family of models, to prove the engine is not tailored to OLMoE. It has different attention and routing.

blocks.title: Assembly lab
blocks.what: Rewriting the hottest kernels in assembly, one at a time. It stays only if the test finds it identical to the C one and the bench finds it faster; the C stays as the fallback for the other CPUs.

numbers.v: the 8-token microkernel did not need assembly: in C with gcc intrinsics it keeps everything in registers; the matmul now at 61% of the no-FMA peak (102 of 166), the kernel at 87% of its ideal flow

the prefill's matmul does 49-53% of the no-FMA peak on one core (87 of 166.5 GFLOP/s); the same instruction flow in assembly with 8 tokens per weight instead of 4 reaches 119.4: 1.34x (prefill estimated 1.15-1.25x)
on Zen 4 the order of independent instructions is worth 20%: mul and add alternated one by one 139 GFLOP/s, grouped 167

questions.text: how much headroom is there under the peak? 1.34x with the 8-token microkernel: built, 1.17-1.23x on the matmul, prefill 1.19-1.30x
FMA in the definition? (Marcello's decision) On this Zen 4 the FMA peak equals mul+add; the 8-token flow with FMA goes 1.19x
do more lanes (32 or 64) unblock the sum chain on one thread?

blocks.title: Metal, and two GPUs together
blocks.what: The Macs (Metal), always as a module, always with the same tokens as the CPU; and a machine with a dedicated and an integrated GPU using both (question 87): today the engine takes the dedicated one and leaves the integrated idle. The integrated GPU alone moved to R1 (the roadmap of 2026-10-03).

questions.text: the dedicated and the integrated GPU together: can the integrated take the work the dedicated cannot hold, reading the RAM in place, with the same bits?

blocks.title: A team of small models
blocks.what: Question 86: can three diverse 1-3B models match one ~7B, at fewer bytes read a token? Placed after rung 2: then the engine runs two families exactly, and a 1-3B model is what a below-average machine holds.
